source.title: The Interpolation Phase Transition in Neural Networks: Memorization and Generalization under Lazy Training

record.tranche_reason: Tests how test error changes with width in an interpolating neural tangent model, using a test-error measure and synthetic data.
record.gate_note: The paper proves interpolation for arbitrary responses and characterizes test risk for natural target functions, but does not measure random-label held-out accuracy or chance performance. It does not test the other claim versions. Figure 2 values are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study directly examines whether test error decreases as width increases beyond interpolation, using minimum-norm neural tangent regression on synthetic spherical data. Figures 1–2 establish vanishing training error around Nd/n = 1 and declining test error above that threshold.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate under the stated assumptions: sufficiently overparameterized minimum-norm NT regression has test risk close to infinite-width kernel ridgeless regression, and NT ridge regression is approximated by polynomial ridge regression with an added self-induced regularization term. Extension to nonlinear networks requires suitable initialization and a valid NT approximation.
record.recipe_differences: Studies min-ℓ2 norm regression in a two-layer neural tangent model with random first-layer weights; it does not run the specified standard-training architecture and dataset sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Test error varies with width and sample size; it rapidly decays toward a width-limit at fixed sample size. The paper also reports that the effective polynomial degree depends on sample size and dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: The study proves arbitrary-response interpolation under its overparameterization assumptions and characterizes test risk through infinite-width kernel regression and effectively regularized polynomial regression.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overparameterized neural tangent interpolators can have prediction risk close to a polynomial ridge estimator despite fitting arbitrary training responses.

record.problems: The numerical width-sweep values are presented only in figures, with no uncertainty estimates stated. The formal generalization results concern the NT model and an isotropic spherical covariate model; their application to fully nonlinear networks is conditional on the NT approximation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version results are reported. Theorem 3.3 and the other theoretical risk statements are summarized under fits_no_version because they characterize test risk rather than the accuracy-versus-chance behavior in V1 or a separate measured-property relation in V7.

untested.parts: No natural-label versus random-label held-out classification accuracy comparison or chance baseline; arbitrary-response interpolation alone does not test this conjunction.
Standard nonlinear training on MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10 is not tested. The width sweep concerns a linearized neural tangent model with ReLU-derived features and synthetic regression targets.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison; using Adam in Appendix A does not test their relative generalization.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurements or ranking of generalization gaps.
No removal of memorized training examples.

missing.what: Record the training-error transition that anchors the width sweeps: training error vanishes sharply as Nd/n crosses approximately 1, with kernel invertibility appearing at the same transition. The record incorrectly says the interpolation threshold is not quantified in the supplied text.
missing.locator: Figure 1 and Section 2.1 discussion immediately following Figure 2

record.verdict_notes: The record's limits_scope label based solely on using synthetic data and an NT model should be removed: those are boundaries of what was tested, not observed failures of the width effect. The interpolation peak is contextual evidence, not itself V2's claim. Risk equivalence and a shrinking approximation-error bound do not prove monotonic test-error improvement at every width.

versions.untested_parts: The paper establishes arbitrary-label interpolation and separately studies test risk for target-function labels, but does not test held-out performance on random labels or compare natural-label accuracy with chance.

Uses a neural tangent model rather than the specified one-hidden-layer ReLU networks trained on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10; the width sweep uses synthetic spherical data. The exact zero-training-error threshold is not quantified in the supplied text.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
No sharpness or other measured-property ranking of generalization gaps.
